19745-something-of-men-i-have-known-with:
Adlai E. Stevenson served as Vice President under Grover Cleveland. Something of Men I Have Known gathers his recollections of public life. The contents promise chapters like Cleveland As I Knew Him. Others include A Camp-Meeting Orator and The Sage of the Bar. A piece called The Gentleman from Mississippi recalls Senate figures. The tone is that of an insider telling stories after dinner.

Political memoirs of this kind trade in portraits, not policy. Stevenson had practiced law and politics in Illinois for decades. He knew the men who ran the post-Civil War republic. His sketches preserve their talk, humor, and habits. Historians mine such books for color. Readers get a front-row seat at a vanished Washington.
19961-aboriginal-remains-in-verde-valley:
Cosmos Mindeleff surveyed aboriginal remains in Arizona's Verde Valley. His report appeared in the Bureau of Ethnology's Thirteenth Annual Report. Written history of the region extends back only a few years, he notes. Since the aboriginal inhabitants abandoned it, Apache and Walapai roamed there unhindered. Cliff houses and pueblos stood empty above the river. Mindeleff mapped and described them for science.

The Verde Valley holds some of the Southwest's richest ruins. Mindeleff, brother of Victor, worked the same federal survey tradition. His plans recorded sites before looting thinned them. Montezuma Castle country is his terrain here. The report joins description to careful measurement. It remains a baseline for Verde Valley archaeology.
20120-the-priest-the-woman-and-the-confe:
Father Chiniquy wrote The Priest, the Woman, and the Confessional, a fierce attack on Catholic confession. Chiniquy had been a Catholic priest before he left that church. He then spent years preaching and writing against its teachings. Scripture fills his pages, quoted to back each charge he makes.

One passage cites Ezekiel on sins that fill a land with violence. Chiniquy reads such texts as proof against the confessional itself. The book stirred strong feeling on both sides when it appeared. It remains a stark record of religious conflict in the nineteenth century.
20209-history-of-steam-on-the-erie-canal:
History of Steam on the Erie Canal traces steam power on New York's great waterway. From 1858 to 1862, a first series of steamers proved the idea. Their success sparked wide enthusiasm for steam transport on the canal. That fall, the governor and Canal Board toured by chartered steam-tug.

Public receptions and speeches greeted them at cities along the route. Steam promised faster, cheaper freight than horse-drawn canal boats could give. Yet locks, size, and cost all limited steam's canal future in fact. Readers get a close record of a key shift in American transport.
20307-kate-s-ordeal:
Emma Leslie wrote Kate's Ordeal, a tale for girls of school and sudden change. Kate races to catch her friends before they reach the school gates. She fans herself with her handkerchief and brings great news breathlessly. She is going to London, she tells them with a triumphant glance.

That glance is aimed at Esther Odell, who called her proud and stuck-up. London, to a country schoolgirl, means wonder, risk, and a test of character. Leslie wrote many tales where faith steadies girls in new trials. Young readers get excitement with a clear moral thread running through.
20924-ely-cathedral:
Cardinal de Luxemburg's tomb, built into the north wall, marks one stop in Ely Cathedral. The retro-choir holds Dr. Mill, a Hebrew scholar from Cambridge, who died in 1853. Faint wall paintings with no known tale mark the east wall's close.

Guidebooks in the Bell's Cathedrals set walk readers stone by stone through great churches. Ely's vast nave, lady chapel, and lantern tower star in this volume. Dates, tombs, and carved work unfold in calm, exact order. The book serves walkers in the church and armchair readers alike, keeping Ely's long past in one handy, trusted guide.
20959-mexico-its-ancient-and-modern-civi:
Thanks for photos crowd the front of Mexico, a survey of its ancient and modern civilisation. The Mexican Financial Agency, rail firms, and banks all aided the plates. C. Reginald Enock built his book with help from men on the ground.

Aztec ruins, mines, farms, railways, and politics fill Enock's wide account. He treats Mexico's past glory and its modern push for growth as one tale. British readers then weighed Mexico for trade and travel in its pages. The book stands as a full, dated portrait of the country on the eve of its great revolution.
21097-tom-finch-s-monkey-and-how-he-dine:
John C. Hutcheson gathers five short late Victorian yarns in this volume, opening with a monkey dressed as an officer aboard ship. The pet is presented to a visiting admiral, who invites all the officers to dinner and asks especially for the quiet one. The tale plays the joke out at sea off Callao.

Other pieces explain icebergs and follow a yachting cruise among the Greek islands. There the party saves a Greek's life and meets bandits. A third reports the sea serpent sighted by HMS Daedalus in 1848. A curious cricket match closes the set. Sea humour ties the five together.
21900-the-principles-of-breeding-or-glim:
Better farm animals through science is S. L. Goodale's aim in The Principles of Breeding, published at Boston in 1861. Goodale, secretary of the Maine Board of Agriculture, says farmers lacked a handy book of the principles behind improvement. His subtitle promises glimpses at the physical laws of reproduction in domestic animals. A transcriber's note warns modern readers that neat cattle are cattle of the bovine kind, not tidy dressers.

Goodale writes for working breeders, not scholars, and keeps the book compact. Heredity, selection, and crossing are handled in plain terms for the farm. The volume shows American agriculture reaching for science just before the Civil War. Its ideas, some since refined away, shaped the breeding sheds of its day.
22035-dramatized-rhythm-plays-mother-goo:
John N. Richards published Dramatized Rhythm Plays in 1922 for teachers of young children. The book turns Mother Goose rhymes and old singing games into small plays acted in rhythm. Little Jack Horner, Humpty Dumpty, and Sing a Song of Sixpence all appear. So do See Saw Marjory Daw and Dickory Dickory Dock.

Louise Westwood, who directed music in the Newark public schools, helped with the musical side. Words and tunes came, with permission, from J. Elliott's nursery rhyme settings. The aim was exercise, music, and play in one lesson. Such rhythm work was a proud feature of progressive classrooms in the 1920s.
22040-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-3-january:
The Prairie Farmer had served farm families from Chicago since 1841. This weekly issue, volume 56 number 3, is dated January 19, 1884. Its motto covers the farm, the orchard, and the fireside. Two dollars a year bought news, advice, and letters from working farmers across the Midwest.

One writer tells how he raised his corn yield past ninety bushels an acre by small experiments. Other pages carry market reports, household hints, and questions answered in print. Such weeklies were the internet of their day for country readers. A single surviving issue shows what prairie families worried about, planted, and hoped for in midwinter 1884.
22897-the-ideal:
Two talkers argue about time in The Ideal, a dialogue in an old-fashioned vein. The Friar looks up and echoes his companion. Time is, indeed, he says. Uttering the word time, the Friar argues, must mean asserting something beyond its bare existence. That existence itself he treats as beyond doubt, since without time nothing could be at all.

From that playful knot the talk ranges over what an ideal is and whether it can exist outside minds. The piece belongs to a tradition of philosophical dialogue written for general readers, more fencing match than lecture. Its pleasure lies in watching an abstract word get chased around a room. Readers who enjoy talk-driven pieces will find a curious, mannered performance preserved here.
23157-other-people-s-business-the-romant:
Harriet Lummis Smith inspects a chair in Other People's Business, the romantic career of the practical Miss Dale, published in 1916. Persis has just rescued her furniture, tactfully, from a heavy guest. Her appraising glance at the vacated chair confirms the damage. Front rung sprung, exactly as expected, and Etta West ought to know better.

Persis Dale's practicality is her fortune and her comedy. She runs a boarding world of other people's business while her own romance assembles itself under her nose. Smith keeps the observation at chair-rung level, where character actually shows. The novel offers small-town American comedy of the sunniest kind, with a heroine whose competence the plot must teach her to set down, briefly, for love.

govdocs-archive_org-TheEinsteinHoaxTheDi:
H. E. Retic published The Einstein Hoax in 1997 through his own company in West Caldwell, New Jersey. His target is Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, which he presents as a disastrous intellectual war on common sense.

Retic argues that relativity misled physics and the wider culture, and he presses his case with the certainty of a man correcting a century of error. He writes for general readers rather than physicists, in plain and forceful terms. The book is held as an archive item, without endorsement, as a strong example of popular anti-relativity writing from the 1990s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAAgentsGenera:
Jeff Gerth of the New York Times reported from Washington, on February 7, on a European figure the CIA had protected. Alfred J. Biihler, a Liechtenstein lawyer and businessman linked to fraud and arms deals, had been shielded by the agency from law-enforcement questioning.

The story is a classic of the post-Church Committee press: an intelligence agency placing its assets beyond the reach of investigators, and a reporter documenting the arrangement. Gerth became known for exactly this kind of digging into the borderland of intelligence and money. The single article is preserved from the Times as part of the era's exposure literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CanadaROAdmiral:
Drew Pearson, whose Washington Merry-Go-Round was the most feared column in American politics, turned his column to a book: Jim Bishop's The Day Kennedy Was Shot. Bishop's hour-by-hour reconstruction of November 22, 1963, appeared in 1968 and reached an enormous readership.

A Pearson column on the book put the popular history before the column's own millions, in the syndicated press where most Americans met the assassination's literature. What Pearson praised or disputed sits in the column itself. The piece is preserved as press history: the era's biggest columnist weighing the era's bestselling account of Dallas.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Canale-TNBarAss:
On January 15, 1971, a Tennessee prosecutor named Canale addressed the Tennessee Bar Association, and this transcript preserves the speech. His subject, in the part that survives most clearly, is Memphis geography: the rooming house at 422 and a half South Main Street, near the Illinois Central station.

That rooming house overlooks the Lorraine Motel, and its bathroom window is where the state said James Earl Ray fired the shot that killed Martin Luther King Jr. A prosecutor describing the scene to fellow lawyers, three years on, was still explaining the ground the case stood on. The transcript is legal oratory preserved for researchers of the King prosecution.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClementsManning:
Manning C. Clements was a Dallas FBI agent, a twenty-three-year veteran of the Bureau, and one of the agents who interviewed Lee Harvey Oswald in custody. This statement summarizes his Warren Commission deposition of April 8, 1964.

Oswald was interrogated for hours across the weekend of November 22 to 24, with no recording and no lawyer, and the agents' later testimony is the main record of what he said. Clements' deposition therefore carries weight out of proportion to its length: it is a participant's sworn account of the interrogation room. The summary is preserved for researchers working through the Oswald interviews.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PresidentialPro: nsia-PresidentialProtection Presidential Protection: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PublicityOswald:
An FBI memorandum dated November 24, 1963, two days after the assassination, carries the heading 'Jack Leon Ruby / Lee Harvey Oswald — Victim.' It was written following Mr. Belmont's instructions and kept in file 44-1639. It records Police Chief Jesse Curry's assurance about the case. Curry said the televised Dallas police appearances in the Oswald case were hurting the possibility of prosecution.

That Sunday, Ruby shot Oswald in the police basement, on television. A memo worrying about publicity and prosecution, written the same weekend, shows officials already feared the cameras. Curry's assurance and Belmont's interest mark the bureau tracking a local chief's media problem as it became a national one.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaidsOfficial_R:
Andrew H. Malcolm reported for the New York Times from Washington on June 24, in a story whose internal dates point to 1973. His subject is violent drug raids against innocent people, found to be widespread. In Miami, residents were handcuffed and held at gunpoint while their homes were ransacked, in raids meant for someone else. Such raids, the story reports, happened once or twice a month.

Wrong-door raids were the drug war's recurring scandal. Malcolm's dispatch counts them, describes the victims' treatment, and names the pattern as policy's cost. The story preserves names, places, and the victims' accounts in a national paper's record. It also shows the early 1970s press beginning to audit drug enforcement itself, not merely to report its seizures.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TattlerNational: Loran Eugene Hall moved through the edges of the Kennedy assassination story for years. The National Tattler article titled The Elusive Mr. Hall follows Hall, who also used the Cuban cover name Lorenzo Eugenio Pascillo, and tracks his movements in 1975. Tabloid coverage kept figures like Hall before the public long after the official investigations ended. The piece shows that fringe of the case as popular papers presented it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WBAL_WBAL: WBAL - a broadcast call sign - titles this declassified US government document at the Internet Archive. The catalog offers no date, no context, no content. Public text not located. A call sign filed among government papers.
govdocs-archive_org-the-papal-origins-of: An article from Historicist.com argues that preterism began with the papacy. Preterism is a school of prophetic reading that treats many Bible prophecies as already fulfilled in the ancient past. The historicist writer behind the piece presents that origin as a Catholic strategy against Protestant teaching. The article serves readers of prophecy debates, where the history of an idea is itself used as a weapon against it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th:
General Carlos Prats had led Chile's army before General Augusto Pinochet, and he was killed with his wife Sofía Cuthbert in Buenos Aires in 1974. The National Security Archive marked fifty years since that bombing in October 2024. Peter Kornbluh edited the document compilation it posted.

The posting calls the killing the Pinochet regime's first act of international terrorism. It includes CIA intelligence reports and the judicial confession of Michael Townley, the Chilean secret police operative who built and placed the bomb. Together the records trace one murder from the order to the courtroom admission.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Critical infrastructure means the systems so vital that their loss would debilitate American security, health, or the economy. This Cyber Vault posting, dated October 22, 2020, reviews President Donald Trump's executive orders on protecting those systems. Homeland Security's own definition frames the discussion.

Trump's presidency produced a high volume of executive orders, and they offer a clear view of his approach. The period also saw Congress create the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency by law. Reading the orders together shows how one administration used its direct pen-and-phone powers on power grids, networks, and other vital assets.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Ira:
For decades the State Department's official history of the 1953 Iran coup whitewashed the American and British roles. Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, number 598, published in June 2017, on the long-awaited replacement volume. The department finally released an updated official history.

Formerly secret documents from State and the CIA supply new information on how the covert operation was planned and carried out. Contemporaneous analyses show what officials thought at the time. An official history correcting itself is a notable event: it means the government's own historians now tell a story closer to what the secret files always showed.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p: Presidential transitions are the moments when one American administration hands power to the next, and foreign rivals take the new president's measure. A National Security Archive briefing book page gathers its Russia material under one heading. It covers Putin, Clinton, and the transition years. In those years Bill Clinton left office and Vladimir Putin rose in Moscow. The evidence here is the page capture itself, so the entry works as a signpost to the Archive's wider record on how Washington and Moscow reset their relationship at the century's turn.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
On November 25, 1975, secret police chiefs from across South America's Southern Cone gathered in Santiago, Chile, at the invitation of Pinochet's intelligence service, DINA. A National Security Archive posting on November 26, 2025, fifty years later, returns to that meeting and to the network it created: Operation Condor.

The agenda said the new body should work like Interpol, but aimed at subversion. Delegations from Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Paraguay, and Uruguay spent three days agreeing to hunt each other's enemies across borders. Kidnappings and murders on foreign soil followed for years. Readers get the founding scene in detail, drawn from the confidential record, and a clear view of how state terror became a shared, cross-border system.

Operation Condor, the pact among South America's military regimes to hunt each other's enemies across borders, reached far beyond the region's dissidents. A National Security Archive briefing book page records one of its most chilling targets: officials of Amnesty International, the human rights organization, marked for liquidation in the network's own language. Only the page capture is preserved in this entry's evidence. Even so, the headline documents how a cross-border terror system viewed the world's best-known human rights monitors: not as neutrals, but as enemies to be killed.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Archive_Hist:
On December 1, 2020, four organizations sued President Donald Trump to stop any destruction of presidential records during the transition to the Biden administration. The plaintiffs were the National Security Archive, two national historians' associations, and Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, and their suit invoked the Presidential Records Act.

That law makes a president's records public property, not personal property, and sets rules for keeping them. The groups feared that a chaotic transition, and a president already known for tearing up papers, could cost the country part of its own history. Filing suit before any destruction could be proved was the point: records cases are usually lost once the records are gone. The posting explains the claims and why historians went to court alongside lawyers.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Imminen: On May 30, 2019, the National Security Archive warned of an imminent threat to Guatemala's Historical Archive of the National Police, the AHPN. That archive holds millions of police records from the civil war and has supplied evidence for human rights trials; its staff and independence came under government pressure in this period. The posting belongs to a series of Archive alerts about the collection's safety. Readers following the archive's fate will find here the alarm at its sharpest, sounded by the institution that helped bring the records to light.
history-of-the-mackenzies-with-genealogi: This thorough history traces the great Mackenzie clan of Scotland. Proud chiefs, fierce battles, and full genealogies fill its pages. Highland heritage is recorded here in impressive detail. A rich treasure for clan researchers and descendants.
john-m-synge-a-few-personal-recollection: John Masefield recalls John Millington Synge — the Playboy of the Western World — with personal warmth. His recollections and notes paint the Irish dramatist vividly. A poet's tribute to a fellow poet. Aran Islands summers and Abbey Theatre nights live in his memoir.

ridgway-of-montana-a-story-of-to-day-in-: William MacLeod Raine's novel about Ridgway of Montana: a modern Western hero, engineer and fighter, in the mining country. Action, romance, and the author's brisk pace fill a story of today. Popular Western fiction at its most entertaining.
right-royal: Poet Laureate John Masefield brings his love of the English countryside to this novel of horse racing. Masefield writes of horses with rare understanding, making the racing world vivid even for readers who have never seen a track.
robert-louis-stevenson-a-record-an-estim: A 1905 biography and appreciation of Robert Louis Stevenson by Alexander H. Japp, who knew the author. Written just a decade after Stevenson's death, it captures how his first readers saw him.
speeches-literary-and-social: The public voice of Charles Dickens: speeches given at banquets, charities, and literary dinners across his career. An essential companion for anyone who loves the man behind the books.
the-essays-or-counsels-civil-and-moral: Francis Bacon's Essays, first published in 1597 and expanded over his lifetime, are short meditations on the art of living and ruling. Truth, ambition, friendship, envy, travel, gardens: Bacon takes up each subject in crisp, quotable sentences packed with practical wisdom. One of the founding works of the English essay, it has been mined for maxims by readers for more than four hundred years.

Winter, published in 1888, gathers the winter entries from Henry Thoreau's great journal. H. Blake, Thoreau's friend and editor, drew them from the journals Thoreau kept for over twenty years. The full journal ran to fourteen volumes in print.

Thoreau walks Concord's ponds and woods through snow, ice, and thaw, noting every track and bird. Walden Pond in winter, woodchucks, owls, and the first hints of spring all pass his keen eye. His entries mix plain fact with sudden poetry. For readers new to the journal, this seasonal volume is a gentle and beautiful entry point.
